name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q01 - Role of ethylene in fruit ripening

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ethylene is a gaseous plant growth regulator (phytohormone) synthesized in large amounts by tissues undergoing senescence and ripening fruits.

Step 2: Evaluation
One of the primary physiological effects of ethylene is the promotion of fruit ripening. It enhances the respiration rate during the ripening of climacteric fruits (known as the respiratory climactic), which accelerates softening, colour change, and sweetness.

Step 3: Application
Because ethylene accelerates rather than retards or slows down ripening in fruits such as tomatoes and apples, it is used commercially (often as ethephon) to hasten fruit ripening.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Ethylene is used for hastening of ripening of fruits.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q02 - Plant growth regulator present in coconut water

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cytokinins are plant growth hormones that promote cell division (cytokinesis). Natural cytokinins are synthesized in regions where rapid cell division occurs, such as root apices, developing shoot buds, and young fruits.

Step 2: Evaluation
Coconut water (liquid endosperm of coconut) is a well-known natural source of zeatin, a naturally occurring cytokinin, and was historically used in plant tissue culture media to stimulate cell division.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Coconut water contains cytokinin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q03 - Hormone that overcomes apical dominance

questiontext.text: The affect of apical dominance can be overcome by which of the following hormone:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Apical dominance is the phenomenon in which the growing apical bud inhibits the growth of lateral (axillary) buds. This inhibition is caused by auxin (IAA) produced at the shoot apex.

Step 2: Evaluation
Cytokinins act antagonistically to auxin with respect to apical dominance. Application of cytokinin promotes the growth of lateral shoots and helps overcome the inhibitory effect of the apical bud.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The effect of apical dominance can be overcome by cytokinin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q04 - Matching plant hormones with their functions and sources

questiontext.text:
Match the following:

A. IAAi. Herring sperm DNA
B. ABAii. Bolting
C. Ethyleneiii. Stomatal closure
D. GAiv. Weed-free lawns
E. Cytokininsv. Ripening of fruits

Options:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each plant growth regulator has characteristic physiological roles and historical sources of discovery.

Step 2: Evaluation
Auxins (such as IAA and synthetic auxins like 2,4-D) are used to kill dicotyledonous weeds and prepare weed-free lawns (A matches iv). Abscisic acid (ABA) stimulates the closure of stomata under water stress (B matches iii). Ethylene promotes the ripening of fruits (C matches v). Gibberellic acid (GA) promotes bolting, i.e., internode elongation just prior to flowering in rosette plants (D matches ii). Cytokinins (specifically kinetin) were first isolated from autoclaved herring sperm DNA (E matches i).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A – iv, B – iii, C – v, D – ii, E – i.

answer.text: A – iv, B – iii, C – v, D – ii, E – i
A – v, B – iii, C – iv, D – ii, E – i
A – iv, B – i, C – iv, D – iii, E – ii
A – v, B – iii, C – ii, D – i, E – iv

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q05 - Reason for wrapping apples in waxed paper

questiontext.text: Apples are generally wrapped in waxed paper to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
After harvesting, fruits continue to respire aerobically using atmospheric oxygen (\(\text{O}_2\)), which accelerates ripening and leads to senescence and spoilage.

Step 2: Evaluation
Wrapping apples in waxed paper creates a barrier that restricts the entry of \(\text{O}_2\). Limiting oxygen availability reduces the rate of aerobic respiration and slows down ethylene-mediated over-ripening, thereby extending shelf life.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Apples are wrapped in waxed paper to prevent aerobic respiration by checking the entry of \(\text{O}_2\).

answer.text: Prevent aerobic respiration by checking the entry of \(\text{O}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q06 - Parameters used to measure plant growth

questiontext.text: Growth can be measured in various ways. Which of these can be used as parameters to measure growth

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At the cellular level, growth is primarily a consequence of an increase in the amount of protoplasm. Because measuring protoplasm directly is difficult, growth is measured by several observable parameters proportional to it.

Step 2: Evaluation
Common parameters used to measure plant growth include increase in fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume, and cell number or cell size. For example, a single maize root apical meristem can give rise to more than 17,500 new cells per hour, whereas cells in a watermelon may increase in size up to 3,50,000 times. Growth of a pollen tube is measured in terms of its length.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Increase in cell number, increase in cell size, and increase in length and weight are all valid parameters to measure growth.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q07 - Meaning of synergistic action of hormones

questiontext.text: The term synergistic action of hormones refers to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plant growth regulators (PGRs) can interact either synergistically or antagonistically in regulating plant growth and development.

Step 2: Evaluation
Synergistic action occurs when two hormones act together and contribute to the same physiological function, producing a combined or enhanced effect (for example, auxin and cytokinin acting together in cell division and differentiation, or auxin and gibberellin promoting stem elongation). By contrast, when two hormones produce opposite effects, their interaction is termed antagonistic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Synergistic action of hormones refers to when two hormones act together and contribute to the same function.

answer.text: When two hormones act together but bring about opposite effects.
When two hormones act together and contribute to the same function.
When one hormone affects more than one function.
When many hormones bring about any one function.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q08 - Definition of plasticity in plant growth

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plants follow different developmental pathways in response to their environment or phases of life to form different kinds of structures. This ability is called plasticity.

Step 2: Evaluation
A classic example of environmental plasticity is heterophylly in buttercup (Ranunculus), where the shapes of leaves produced in air differ from those produced in water. Similarly, developmental heterophylly is seen in cotton, coriander, and larkspur, where juvenile and adult leaves differ in shape. Thus, plasticity reflects that plant development is dependent on the environment (and developmental phase).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Plasticity in plant growth means that plant development is dependent on the environment.

answer.text: Plant development is dependent on the environment

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q09 - Hormone sprayed on sugarcane to increase yield

questiontext.text: To increase sugar production in sugarcanes, they are sprayed with

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gibberellins promote stem elongation (internode elongation) in plants.

Step 2: Evaluation
Sugarcane stores carbohydrate as sugar in its stems. Spraying sugarcane crops with gibberellins increases the length of the stem, which increases the total biomass and sugar yield by as much as 20 tonnes per acre.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
To increase sugar production in sugarcanes, they are sprayed with gibberellin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q10 - Hormone to which ABA acts antagonistic

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Abscisic acid (ABA) is primarily a plant growth inhibitor that promotes seed dormancy and inhibits seed germination and growth.

Step 2: Evaluation
Gibberellic acid (GA) acts as a growth promoter that breaks seed dormancy and stimulates seed germination (for example, by inducing \(\alpha\)-amylase synthesis in barley aleurone layers). In most situations, ABA acts as an antagonist to gibberellic acid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
ABA acts antagonistic to gibberellic acid (written in the source as Gibberlic acid).

Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Based on the number of flowering and fruiting cycles in a plant's lifetime, plants are classified as monocarpic or polycarpic.

Step 2: Evaluation
Monocarpic plants flower and set seeds only once in their lifetime and then die. Examples include annuals (such as wheat and rice), biennials (such as radish and carrot), and certain perennials like bamboo (which flowers once after 50–100 years and dies).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Monocarpic plants are those which flower once and die.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_MCQ_Q12 - Site of photoperiod perception in plants

questiontext.text: The photoperiod in plants is perceived at

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Photoperiodism is the response of plants to periods of day and night, particularly in the induction of flowering.

Step 2: Evaluation
While the shoot apices modify themselves into flowering apices prior to flowering, they cannot perceive photoperiods by themselves. The site of perception of light/dark duration (photoperiod) is the leaves. Upon perceiving the appropriate photoperiod, a hormonal substance (florigen) migrates from the leaves to the shoot apices to induce flowering.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The photoperiod in plants is perceived at the leaves.
